body:
Please read this part twice. Do not begin this plan on day one. Begin it after you have sat in front of your doctor with two things in your hand: this plan, and your blood report dated 27 May 2026.

Here is exactly why, in plain words. Your report shows HbA1c 7.00% and a mean glucose of 154 mg/dL. On that same report, the lab prints its own criteria: 5.7 to 6.4 percent is the prediabetes band, and 6.5 percent and above is the diabetes band. On your intake form you have written prediabetes. I am not the person to settle that difference and neither is a diet plan. Your doctor is. I am only telling you what the paper says, and that the paper and the form do not match.

The second thing: you told us the report was within 30 days. It is dated 27 May 2026 and your form came in on 18 August 2026. That is 83 days. Three months is long enough for numbers to move, in either direction. Your doctor may well want fresh tests before you cut your food down to 1400 calories a day.

There are two more lines on that report worth showing them: LDL 110.71 (report's mark is under 100) and HDL 39.51 (report's mark is above 40), which puts your cholesterol-to-HDL ratio at 4.29 against a mark of under 3.5. With blood pressure already on your list, your doctor should see all of it together.

So, three questions to ask them, and please write the answers down:
1. Is a 1400 calorie plan the right one for me, starting now?
2. Do I need repeat blood tests before I start?
3. Is there anything in my medicines that needs looking at now?

That third one is theirs to answer, not mine, and not yours. Nothing in this plan asks you to change any medicine you are taking.

This is a gate, not a disclaimer. Doctor first. Then day one.
heading: Before you start

body:
Your day is 1400 calories, with 130g protein, about 110g carbohydrate, about 48g fat, and 30g or more of fibre.

That splits across your three meals the way you asked for them:
Breakfast, late: about 400 calories, 35g protein
Lunch, the heaviest meal: about 620 calories, 55g protein
Dinner, the lightest meal: about 380 calories, 40g protein

Now the honest arithmetic, so you can see where any number comes from.

At your height, weight and age, your body burns roughly 1975 calories a day doing absolutely nothing - lying still, all day. That is the starting figure. Add an office job, a sedentary day, under 2000 steps, and you land at roughly 2370 calories a day burned.

Eat 1400 against 2370 and you are short by about 970 calories a day. Body fat works out to roughly 7700 calories per kilo. So 970 a day for 30 days is about 29,000 calories, which is about 3.8 kg of fat in a month. That is what the food alone does.

The movement plan is what closes the rest of the gap. Roughly 300 calories a day of activity takes your burn to about 2670, and the daily shortfall to about 1270. Over 30 days that is roughly 38,000 calories, about 4.9 kg. That is where the 5 kg comes from - not from the food, from the food plus the walking.

I am not promising you 5 kg. I am showing you the sum and what it rests on: eating the plan on most days, not perfect days, and actually doing the movement. Real bodies do not run like calculators. The first week or two often shows a bigger drop because of water, and then it settles. Some months will be slower. You asked for 5 to 6 kg a month - 5 is what this arithmetic supports with movement. 6 is not something these numbers show, and I would rather tell you that now than have you feel like a failure at the end of month one.

The honest spread: whichever options you pick, a day lands between 1,334 and 1,460 calories. That is a 9% spread, so any combination really does give you the same day — unlike a plan that just says so. A fully vegetarian day averages 1,419 calories and 129g protein, which is the same day again. You never lose protein by skipping the chicken.
heading: Your numbers

body:
Three meals a day. Breakfast, lunch, dinner. No snacks built in, because you asked for three meals.

Under each meal you will find seven options. Pick any one. That is the whole system. You do not have to follow a Monday-to-Sunday chart, you do not have to plan ahead, and you do not have to eat things in order. Open the list for that meal, see what is in the kitchen, pick one, eat it.

Any breakfast option works with any lunch option and any dinner option. They are all built to land on the same day total, so you cannot get it wrong by mixing.

The shape of the day is the one you asked for:
Breakfast is late - you wake at 6 to 7 AM and eat late, so eat it late. That is fine.
Lunch is the biggest meal, the one you look forward to.
Dinner is the lightest, and lighter dinners usually sit better at night anyway.

Every option is built for 0 to 10 minutes of cooking on a gas stove, with a mixer if you need it. Nothing here needs an oven, an air fryer or a microwave. Nothing here uses cabbage or cauliflower.

One small thing that matters: eat all three. Skipping breakfast or dinner to 'save' calories is the single quickest way to end up eating something out of a packet at 9 PM.

Two shortcuts that keep every option inside ten minutes, and they are not cheating: buy your idli and dosa batter ready-made, and buy your curd in a tub. Nothing in this plan asks you to ferment or set anything overnight.
heading: How to use this

body:
You said you eat non-veg once a week, and you named chicken. So the plan is built exactly that way.

The options marked for chicken or fish are for one meal, one day a week. Pick the day that suits you - most people put it on a Sunday lunch. Choose one such option, eat it, and that is your non-veg for the week.

Every other meal in the week runs on egg, curd, paneer, dal and vegetables. Those are all things you already eat and already like, so nothing new has to enter your kitchen.

And this is worth saying clearly: your 130g of protein a day is fully covered without chicken. The eggs, curd, paneer and dal do that work on their own. The weekly chicken is there because you enjoy it, not because the plan would fall short without it. If a week goes by and you do not feel like it, nothing breaks.
heading: Chicken and fish

body:
About 3 teaspoons of added oil a day. That is for everything - tadka, the sabzi, the pan. Around 15g in total.

The measurements, so there is no guessing:
One level teaspoon of any oil or ghee is 5g and about 45 calories.
One level tablespoon of grated coconut is about 10g and carries about 4g of fat, so count it as oil, not as a garnish.

You have sunflower, rice bran, coconut, cow ghee and butter at home. All five can stay in the kitchen. But because your LDL is on the high side and your HDL is on the low side, make rice bran or sunflower your everyday cooking oil - that is the one that goes into the daily dal and sabzi. Keep coconut oil and ghee for the dishes that genuinely need them, a couple of times a week, not as the default. Butter is an occasional thing, not a daily one. Nobody is asking you to throw anything away.

The part that decides whether this works: measure it. Take a small katori, put your day's 3 teaspoons into it in the morning, and cook from that katori all day. Never tip the tin straight into the hot kadai. A two-second pour is very easily 3 teaspoons on its own, and then the whole day's fat is gone before lunch.

You already listed oily food as something you avoid. This is just the number that goes with that instinct.
heading: How much oil, exactly

body:
You have 1 tea and 2 coffees a day, and your first one is on an empty stomach in the morning. The tea and coffee themselves are fine and can stay - just keep them without sugar, and remember that milk and sugar in three cups adds up quietly across a day.

There is one thing you need to raise with your doctor, and it is a known, well-documented interaction, not a theory: coffee can interfere with how much levothyroxine your body absorbs when the two are taken close together. Your Eltroxin is a levothyroxine tablet, and your first coffee is on an empty stomach in the morning - which is exactly the window this applies to.

What I am not going to do is tell you to move your tablet, change when you take it, or change anything about the dose. That is entirely your doctor's call and it should be made by them, with your reports in front of them.

What I am asking you to do is add one question to the list for that appointment: 'I drink coffee first thing in the morning. How long a gap do you want between my tablet and my first cup?' Write down what they say and follow that, not this page.

Until you have that answer, carry on exactly as you are doing now. Do not start rearranging your medicine on your own.
heading: Your tea and coffee

body:
You have told us about bloating, and you are going once a day. This plan is built to carry about 30g of fibre a day - from the dal, the vegetables, the salads and the whole grains - which is more fibre than most people are used to. That is good for you, for your digestion and for your blood sugar. But fibre has one rule attached to it.

Fibre needs water. Fibre works by absorbing water and making the stool soft and bulky so it moves easily. If the fibre goes up and the water does not, it does the opposite - the stool gets harder and drier, and you feel more blocked and more bloated than before you started. This is the single most common reason a healthy diet makes someone's stomach worse in week one.

So: 2.5 to 3 litres of water a day. You are at 2 to 3 now, so push to the upper end and stay there. Practical way to do it - a one-litre bottle on your desk, finished by lunch, refilled, finished by evening, and a third around dinner. Do not try to drink it all in the last two hours of the day.

For the bloating specifically, four things that actually help:
Eat slower and chew properly. Bloating is very often swallowed air, especially at a big lunch eaten fast.
Sit and eat, do not eat standing or walking.
A glass of buttermilk or plain curd with lunch settles most stomachs.
A 10-minute slow walk after lunch and after dinner. It helps digestion and it counts towards your movement.

Give it a fortnight. Bloating that comes from more fibre usually settles as your gut adjusts. Bloating that gets worse, or comes with pain, is a doctor conversation, not a diet one.
heading: Constipation and bloating

body:
Blood pressure is on your list, so salt matters here - but the salt problem in an Indian kitchen is almost never the salt in the dal.

It is these:
Pickle. One spoon can carry more salt than an entire home-cooked meal.
Papad. One papad is a surprising amount of salt for something that feels like nothing.
Packeted namkeen, mixture, chips, bhujia. This is the biggest one for most people.
Sauces - tomato ketchup, soy sauce, chilli sauce, packaged chutneys.
Ready masala mixes, instant noodles, packet soups, and anything that comes in a sachet promising a meal in two minutes.

Practical version: salt goes in while cooking, and the salt shaker does not come to the table. Pickle and papad become an occasional thing, not a daily accompaniment. And when you buy anything packaged, the useful habit is simply to buy less of it, rather than to start reading labels you will get tired of reading.

One thing to keep doing exactly as you are: you use iodised salt daily. Continue. Iodine matters for you, and iodised salt is the main way most Indian households get it. Do not switch to rock salt, black salt, sea salt or any 'low sodium' substitute on your own - the low-sodium ones swap in potassium, which is a conversation for your doctor given your blood pressure, not a supermarket decision.

Cooking at home, which this whole plan does, has already cut most of your salt without you doing anything else.
heading: Salt

body:
You named cravings as your biggest challenge. So let us treat it as a real problem with a real method, not with the word 'willpower'.

First, the thing that does most of the work, and you will not feel it happening: protein at every single meal. 35g at breakfast, 55g at lunch, 40g at dinner. Protein keeps you full for hours in a way that rice and chapati alone do not. Most evening cravings are not a character flaw, they are a lunch that had no protein in it. Eat the meals as written and you will find the 5 PM pull is smaller before you have had to fight it once.

Second, know your own timing. For most women with a desk job, it hits between 4 and 6 PM, and again after dinner. Yours may differ - watch for a week and you will know. A craving you saw coming is much easier to handle than one that ambushes you.

Third, what to actually eat when it hits. Not nothing - something. Keep these in the house so the choice is already made:
Curd or plain Greek yogurt
Boiled eggs, two, already boiled and sitting in the fridge
Roasted chana
Buttermilk
Cucumber and a katori of fruit
Green tea, which handles the 'I want something' feeling more often than you would expect

Fourth, what not to keep in the house. Biscuits, namkeen packets, mithai, chocolate, cold drinks. Not because they are forbidden, but because a packet in the kitchen is a decision you have to win every evening, and a packet you never bought is a decision you never have to make. Willpower is a small budget. Do not spend it on your own kitchen shelf.

Fifth, the ten-minute rule. When it hits: one full glass of water, then wait ten minutes. A fair number of cravings are thirst or boredom and they simply leave. If after ten minutes it is still there, eat one of the things from the list above, properly, sitting down.

And sixth, the one that keeps people in the game: if you eat the sweet, eat it. Then the next meal happens exactly as planned. Do not skip dinner to make up for it, do not double the walk as punishment, do not write off the week. One sweet does not undo anything. A week of skipping meals to atone for one sweet undoes plenty.

One last thing worth knowing: two coffees on a nearly empty stomach with breakfast pushed late is a setup for a hard hunger crash later in the day. Eating your late breakfast rather than letting it slide into lunch will take the edge off your afternoon.
heading: Cravings

body:
You start in two days, and you have told us your motivation is low. Good - that is honest, and it is exactly why week one is going to be small.

Here is everything you have to get right in week one. It is four things.

1. See the doctor before day one, with the report and this plan. This one is not optional and not negotiable. Everything else waits behind it.

2. Eat three meals. Pick any option from each list. Do not skip breakfast, do not skip dinner, do not try to be clever and eat less than the plan says. Eating the plan is the win.

3. Drink the water. 2.5 to 3 litres. Bottle on the desk, refilled twice.

4. Walk after lunch and after dinner. Ten minutes each, slow. That is it for week one. You are under 2000 steps a day right now, so the movement plan builds from here - but week one is only these two short walks. One note, because of your varicose veins: several short walks are better for your legs than one long one, and standing still for long stretches is the thing to avoid. If your legs ache or swell, that goes to your doctor.

That is the whole of week one.

Now, what you have permission to ignore, completely, for seven days: the oil measuring, the salt list, the fibre detail, the craving strategy, the weekly chicken, the arithmetic in 'Your numbers'. All of it is there and all of it matters later. None of it matters in week one. Read it when you are ready.

Do not weigh yourself daily. Weigh once, on day one, in the morning after the bathroom, and then not again until the same morning next week. Daily weight goes up and down with water and salt and sleep, and watching it every morning has ended more plans than any biscuit ever has.

The goal for week one is not weight loss. It is seven days of three meals and two short walks, so that in week two this is already something you do, instead of something you are trying to start.
heading: Week one

body: The food gets you about 3.8 kg a month. The movement plan is what takes it to 5, and it is a separate plan in the app under Workouts. It is built around walking in short bouts after meals rather than a gym, because of your knees and your varicose veins. Please have your doctor clear the walking volume at the same appointment.
heading: Your movement plan
